entries.title: Why alarm features matter
entries.body: Many GI consultations are for functional (non-organic) symptoms, yet about **20% of all cancers** arise in the GI tract. The clinician's main task is therefore to separate organic disease from functional symptoms, and alarm features are the tool for doing so.

entries.title: Vomiting: how it is triggered
entries.body:
- **Vomiting centres** lie in the reticular formation of the medulla. They are stimulated by the **chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)** and by the **vagus**; drugs, motion sickness and metabolic causes can stimulate these zones directly.
- Vomiting is usually preceded by two phases:
  - **Nausea**, with autonomic features (salivation, pallor, sweating).
  - **Retching**, a strong, involuntary, unproductive effort to vomit with contraction of the abdominal muscles.
- Add **vestibular disease** to the CNS causes of vomiting (alongside raised intracranial pressure and migraine).

entries.title: Flatulence
entries.body: Flatulence means excessive wind: belching, abdominal distension, gurgling, or passing flatus per rectum. Increased gas production comes from colonic bacterial breakdown of non-absorbed carbohydrate, a high-fibre diet, and carbonated drinks.

entries.title: Abdominal pain: extra diagnostic clues
entries.body:
- **Porphyria** is another metabolic cause of an apparent "acute abdomen", alongside diabetic ketoacidosis.
- **Epigastric pain:** functional dyspepsia is the commonest diagnosis, but its symptoms can be **identical** to those of peptic ulcer disease.
- **Biliary pain** can be felt in the epigastrium as well as the right hypochondrium. It remits spontaneously and recurs weeks or months later.
- **Peptic ulcer** sometimes presents with right hypochondrial pain.
- Chronic, constant hypochondrial pain (right or left) in a **well-looking patient** is frequently functional. Right iliac fossa pain may also be functional.

entries.title: Blood per rectum: where is it from?
entries.body:
- Dark blood and clots per rectum **without shock** always come from a lower GI source. An upper GI bleed produces blood per rectum only when it is massive, and then it is usually accompanied by shock.
- Haematochezia usually comes from a lesion distal to the **ligament of Treitz** (duodenojejunal junction). It can also occur with a massive upper GI bleed because of rapid transit.

entries.title: Endoscopy: practical details
entries.body:
- **Sigmoidoscopy** is also used for diarrhoea and change in bowel habit. The **rigid** scope inspects at most 20–25 cm of distal colon; the **flexible** scope can reach the splenic flexure.
- **Colonoscopy:** benign strictures are **dilated**; malignant strictures are **stented**.
- **Balloon enteroscopy** (single or double balloon) can examine the small bowel from the duodenum to the ileum, using specialised enteroscopes in expert centres.
- **Capsule endoscopy:** avoid it if a stricture is suspected.

entries.title: Imaging: extra interpretation points
entries.body:
- **Plain films:** chest as well as abdominal films are used in the acute abdomen; interpretation depends on gas shadows inside and outside the bowel. Plain films can also assess **faecal loading** in constipation. CT is more sensitive than plain films for gallstone and chronic pancreatitis calcification.
- **Ultrasound** in the acute abdomen can also show enlarged mesenteric glands.
- **CT:** oral intraluminal contrast (e.g. Gastrografin) with IV contrast improves diagnosis. CT is sensitive to **small volumes of gas** from a perforated viscus and to **contrast leak** from the gut lumen. In **high-grade** obstruction it is usually diagnostic of both the presence and the cause. It can guide biopsy of tumours or lymph nodes.
- **PET** is also used to detect **recurrent** disease.

entries.title: CT colonography: how it is done
entries.body: CT colonography ("virtual colonoscopy") is performed after CO₂ insufflation into a previously cleansed colon. It is an alternative to colonoscopy for diagnosing colonic mass lesions.

entries.title: Contrast studies
entries.body:
- Gastroscopy replaced the barium meal because it is **more sensitive** and allows **biopsy**.
- **Small bowel follow-through** shows the fold pattern and calibre of the small bowel; dedicated views of the terminal ileum show **early changes of Crohn's disease or TB**.
- **Small bowel enema (enteroclysis):** a tube is passed into the duodenum and a large volume of dilute barium is introduced, to show strictures or adhesions when intermittent obstruction is suspected. It has generally been replaced by **MR enteroclysis**.

entries.title: Two further indications for surgery
Gastric mucus and the functions of acid
entries.body:
- Mucus-secreting cells are present **throughout the stomach** and secrete both mucus and bicarbonate. The mucus is made of glycoproteins called **mucins**.
- Gastric acid is **not essential for digestion**, but it protects against some food-borne infections.
- Other gastric functions: a **reservoir** for food, **emulsification of fat** and mixing of gastric contents.

entries.title: Classifying gastritis and its causes
entries.body:
- Gastritis may be classified by **acuity** (acute vs chronic), by **histology**, or by **etiology**.
- **Gastropathy** (epithelial injury and regeneration with little inflammation) is usually caused by **bile reflux**, **hypovolaemia**, or **chronic congestion** as in portal hypertension.
- Named causes of gastritis:
  - H. pylori gastritis, the **commonest** cause
  - erosive and haemorrhagic gastritis (NSAIDs)
  - autoimmune gastritis
  - viral infection (CMV, herpes simplex)
  - Crohn's disease

entries.title: Acute gastritis: extra points
entries.body:
- Stress gastritis also occurs in **acute myocardial infarction** and **stroke**, as well as after surgery, trauma, burns and CNS injury.
- Most acute gastritis settles within days to weeks, but some cases become recurrent or long-term, i.e. **chronic gastritis**. Over time this raises the risk of gastric ulcer, upper GI bleeding and some gastric neoplasms.

entries.title: Where intestinal metaplasia comes from
entries.body: Gastric metaplasia, usually of the **intestinal type**, occurs almost always in the setting of **atrophic gastritis**. The book's Chapter 4 (p. 72) says intestinal-type gastric cancer arises on intestinal metaplasia; this supplies the missing first link. Chapter 4 here completes the sequence to dysplasia and cancer.

entries.title: Why combination therapy, and who is treated
entries.body:
- **No single drug** is effective against H. pylori on its own, so regimens combine two antibiotics with powerful acid suppression.
- Resistance to metronidazole and clarithromycin is high in some populations, and oral metronidazole frequently causes side-effects.
- **All** patients with duodenal or gastric ulcer who have H. pylori should receive eradication therapy. Treating incidental infection with **no ulcer** is controversial.

topics.title: NSAIDs, erosive gastritis and the drugs

entries.title: NSAID damage: how common, and why it can be missed
entries.body:
- Aspirin inhibits the synthesis of both prostaglandin E2 and **F2-alpha**.
- With recurrent NSAID use (e.g. osteoarthritis) erosive gastritis can become **chronic**, and in alcoholics and chronic NSAID users it may be **completely asymptomatic**.
- Only about **5%** of NSAID users have GI symptoms and **1–2%** a major problem such as a GI bleed.

entries.title: Drug options for acute and erosive gastritis
entries.body:
- Three drug options for erosive and haemorrhagic gastritis: **H2 blockers** (e.g. famotidine, which may be used along with the PPI), **proton pump inhibitors** and **sucralfate**. In the book, sucralfate appears only in the pharmacology table (mainly stress-ulcer prophylaxis).
- Remove risk factors: stop NSAIDs, reduce caffeine, stop alcohol and smoking.

entries.title: Long-term PPI use and bone
entries.src: GIT Others p. 11 (MCQ 24, keyed on p. 12)
entries.body: **Osteoporosis** is a possible complication of chronic (long-term) PPI use. Add it to the PPI adverse effects, after vitamin B12 deficiency.

entries.title: Drugs and bleeding: two qualifiers
entries.body:
- **Even 75 mg/day of aspirin** can produce ulcers, erosions and GI haemorrhage.
- GIT Internal Med states that corticosteroids in the usual therapeutic doses have **no influence on GI haemorrhage** on their own. (Book p. 50 still advises avoiding NSAID–corticosteroid combinations.)

entries.title: Natural history and prognosis
entries.body:
- Any significant GI bleed within the last **48 hours** should be assessed in hospital.
- About **85%** of patients stop bleeding spontaneously within 48 hours; many need no immediate treatment because the blood loss is small.
- Mortality from GI haemorrhage has stayed at **5–12%** despite advances in management, mainly because patients are now older and have more co-morbidity.

entries.title: Resuscitation and history: practical triggers
entries.body:
- **Circulation:** unless there are clear signs of a cardiac cause, give IV fluid to any patient with **cool peripheries and a fast heart rate**.
- **Disability:** common causes of unconsciousness are profound hypoxia, hypercapnia, cerebral hypoperfusion, or recently given sedatives/analgesics.
- **History:** co-morbidity; acid-peptic symptoms; alcoholic liver disease, chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis; anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, steroids, alcohol binge; coagulation disorders. Ask about **epistaxis or haemoptysis** to exclude a non-GI source of the blood.

entries.title: Transfusion and supportive care
entries.body:
- Monitor pulse and BP **half-hourly**; cross-match **2 units** initially. Give plasma expanders or 0.9% saline until blood is available, then restore volume rapidly, preferably with red cell concentrates through large-bore cannulae.
- **Shock** is a trigger for transfusion: pallor, cold nose, systolic BP < 100 mmHg, pulse > 100/min. (The source's haemoglobin threshold is kept for review in R05, not taught here.)
- **Pulse rate and venous pressure** are the best guides to adequate transfusion (the book, p. 51, explains why Hb is not). Insert a **CVP line** if there is organ failure or a high risk of heart failure, and watch for fluid overload, especially in the elderly.
- Manage patients in **high-dependency beds**.
- GIT Internal Med uses a **nasogastric tube** for gastric wash and monitoring of ongoing bleeding in non-variceal bleeding. The book is silent here; for variceal bleeding it treats the tube as selective (p. 315, review point R33).

entries.title: Stigmata of recent haemorrhage
entries.body:
- Endoscopy finds the cause in **80% or more** of cases.
- Stigmata of recent bleeding are a **spurting vessel, active oozing, fresh or organised clot, or black spots**. Their presence means a **higher risk of rebleeding**, which is why they are an indication for endoscopic haemostasis.

entries.title: Endoscopic haemostasis: how each method works
entries.body:
- **Why combine:** dual or triple therapy reduces rebleeding more than monotherapy.
- **Adrenaline injection** gives temporary local tamponade and vasoconstriction: 0.5–1.0 mL aliquots of epinephrine 1:10,000 into four quadrants of the ulcer, within 1–2 mm of the bleeding point. Used **alone** it is less effective than other monotherapies. Its main use in active bleeding is **pre-injection**, to slow bleeding and improve the view before definitive therapy. Sclerosants (e.g. ethanolamine) and thrombogenic agents are less efficacious.
- **Thermal:** contact probes compress the vessel and then coagulate it (coaptive coagulation); the **bipolar probe** is the most widely used. **Argon plasma coagulation** is non-contact: monopolar current delivered through ionised argon gas. Other options are the heater probe and laser.
- **Clips** are the therapy of choice for **obvious arterial bleeding**. Unlike cautery they cause no further tissue damage, and they reduce rebleeding.

entries.title: Specific causes and after-care
entries.body:
- **Mallory–Weiss tear:** caused by a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure. A history of retching **may be absent**. Most bleeds are minor and patients are usually discharged within 24 hours, though the haemorrhage can occasionally be large.
- **After a bleeding ulcer:** continue the PPI for **4 weeks**; always **confirm H. pylori eradication**; if eradication fails, give long-term acid suppression.
- **Bleeding gastric cancer:** bleeds are usually not large, but oozing from the tumour is very difficult to control endoscopically. Surgery is occasionally needed for uncontrolled or repeated bleeding and can usually wait until full evaluation. Radiotherapy is occasionally successful.

entries.title: Antithrombotic drugs during a GI bleed
entries.body:
- Clopidogrel and warfarin are also stopped, but stopping antiplatelets needs urgent discussion with a **cardiologist** (the book, p. 50, gives the thrombosis risk).
- **After PCI**, heparins and clopidogrel increase GI bleeding: give an **IV PPI bolus followed by an infusion**; **platelet infusion** can counter clopidogrel.

topics.title: Acute lower and chronic GI bleeding

entries.title: Lower GI bleeding: sorting the source
entries.body:
- **Unstable patient:** GIT Internal Med performs **nasogastric lavage** (see R33 on nasogastric tubes). Blood in the aspirate identifies an upper GI source; a clear aspirate makes a lower GI source more likely. Then proceed to angiography with embolisation, endoscopic intervention or, in extreme cases, surgery. Each of these both locates and treats the bleeding.
- **Stable patient:** abdominal and pelvic CT with oral contrast is used to look for the cause.
- **Angiography** has a low yield, so it is a test of last resort.

entries.title: Chronic GI blood loss
entries.body:
- The cancers to exclude are particularly **stomach** and **right colon**.
- **Occult blood tests are unhelpful** in this work-up.
- Oesophageal varices usually bleed overtly and **rarely** present as chronic blood loss. **Hookworm** is the most common cause worldwide.
- Do upper endoscopy and colonoscopy **in the same session**. A colonic polyp found at colonoscopy should **not** be assumed to be the cause.
- In frail patients, **unprepared CT** is a reasonable test for colon cancer. Capsule endoscopy yields a diagnosis in **60–85%** but cannot treat.

entries.title: Squamous cell carcinoma under the microscope
entries.body: It is made of **islands of neoplastic squamous cells**. Differentiated tumours also show **epithelial cell nests**.

entries.title: A malignant ulcer can bleed fatally
entries.body: As well as dysphagia and haematemesis, **perforation of the malignant ulcer can cause fatal haemorrhage**.

entries.title: H. pylori to cancer: the last steps
entries.body:
- The sequence continues past intestinal metaplasia: H. pylori gastritis → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → **dysplasia → cancer**. (The atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia step is in Chapter 3 here.)
- GIT Others lists intestinal metaplasia as a **precancerous (dysplastic) lesion** of the stomach.

entries.title: Lauren classification: name and frequency of the two types
entries.body: The intestinal and diffuse types make up the **Lauren classification**: intestinal type **53%**, diffuse type **33%**, unclassified **14%**.

entries.title: The malignant gastric ulcer
entries.body: The ulcer is typically **more than 5 cm** across, with an everted edge, a **necrotic floor** and a **firm base**.

entries.title: Blood spread goes beyond the liver
entries.body: Blood-borne metastases go to the liver and also to the **lung, bone and brain**.

entries.title: Colonic adenomas run in families
entries.body: There is a **well-defined familial predisposition** to colonic adenomas. They predispose to colorectal carcinoma.

entries.title: Tubular vs villous adenoma: size and cancer risk
entries.body:
| | Tubular adenoma | Villous adenoma |
| Size | Small, <1 cm | Large, >2 cm |
| Dysplasia / cancer | Rare | High (about 40%) |
GIT Others' table gives the 40% for adenomas >4 cm; its text gives it for villous adenomas in general.

topics.title: Physiology of fluid and nutrient handling

entries.title: Where intestinal water comes from and why it moves
entries.body:
- Water crosses the epithelium **passively**. It follows osmotic gradients created by **active transport** of electrolytes (Na⁺, Cl⁻) and of other solutes such as sugars and amino acids.
- Most of the ~9 L delivered to the small intestine each day is **endogenous secretion**, not oral intake:
Table: Daily fluid delivered to the small intestine (GIT Internal Med p. 49)
| Source | Volume (mL) |
| Oral intake | 2,000 |
| Salivary secretion | 1,500 |
| Gastric secretion | 2,500 |
| Pancreatic secretion | 1,500 |
| Biliary secretion | 500 |
| Small intestinal secretion | 1,000 |
| Total | 9,000 |

entries.title: Digestive enzymes by source
entries.body:
Amylase breaks starch into oligosaccharides, and brush-border enzymes finish the job: lactase splits lactose into glucose + galactose, and sucrase splits sucrose into glucose + fructose.
Table: Digestive enzymes by source (GIT Internal Med p. 50)
| Source | Enzymes |
| Salivary glands | Amylase, lingual lipase |
| Stomach | Pepsin |
| Pancreas | Amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, elastase, lipase–colipase, phospholipase A2, cholesterol esterase |
| Intestinal mucosa | Enterokinase; disaccharidases (sucrase, maltase, trehalase, α-dextrinase/isomaltase); peptidases (aminooligopeptidase, dipeptidase) |

entries.title: Where nutrients are absorbed
entries.body:
The site of disease predicts the deficiency:
- **Duodenum and jejunum:** calcium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, folate, the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and lipids, monosaccharides and small peptides.
- **Ileum:** **vitamin B12** and **bile salts and acids** (also vitamin C, folate, vitamins D and K, magnesium). Many other nutrients can be absorbed here depending on transit time.
- **Large intestine:** water, sodium, chloride, potassium, short-chain fatty acids, vitamin K and biotin.

entries.title: Osmotic and secretory diarrhoea: the mechanism behind the lists
entries.body:
- **Osmotic:** usually a poorly absorbable carbohydrate or a **divalent ion** (e.g. magnesium). The high luminal osmolality draws water into the duodenum and jejunum to make chyme isotonic. Na⁺ then follows the water into the lumen down its concentration gradient, and this Na⁺ pulls in further water.
- **Secretory laxatives** (examples for the book's "laxatives"): ricinoleic acid (castor oil) and dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate.

entries.title: Why oral rehydration works even in cholera
entries.body: Even while cholera toxin (via cAMP) drives chloride secretion from the crypts, villus cells can still absorb sodium, and with it water and chloride, through **coupled uptake of sodium with glucose or amino acids**. Oral rehydration solution uses this intact pathway.

entries.title: Acute infectious diarrhoea: clues from the exposure
entries.body:
Table: Vehicle and classic pathogens (GIT Internal Med p. 55)
| Vehicle | Classic pathogens |
| Water | Vibrio cholerae, Giardia |
| Poultry | Salmonella |
| Seafood and shellfish (e.g. sushi) | Salmonella and Shigella |
| Canned vegetables or fruits | Clostridium species |
| Cheese, milk | Listeria species |
| Hospitalisation, antibiotics or chemotherapy | C. difficile |
| Animal-to-person (pets) | Salmonella, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium |
The laboratory side of Salmonella and Campylobacter is added in Chapter 7.

entries.title: Clostridium difficile colitis
entries.body:
The book names C. difficile only as a cause. GIT Internal Med adds:
- **Pathogenesis:** antibiotics disrupt the normal flora; C. difficile colonises the colon and releases **toxins** that cause mucosal damage and inflammation (originally called pseudomembranous colitis).
- **Diagnosis:** diarrhoea (≥ 3 unformed stools in 24 h) **or** radiographic ileus/toxic megacolon, **plus** a positive stool C. difficile toxin test **or** pseudomembranes at colonoscopy/pathology.
- **Treatment:** stop the offending antibiotic. **Metronidazole** is the drug of choice for mild infection; **vancomycin** for more severe episodes; **fidaxomicin** (a macrocyclic antibiotic) is more active than vancomycin.
- Probiotics are promising for prevention and treatment. **Faecal microbiota transplantation** is reserved for refractory C. difficile colitis.

entries.title: Chronic diarrhoea: think of the patient group
entries.body:
Table: Chronic diarrhoea in specific patient groups (GIT Internal Med p. 59)
| Patient group | Causes to consider |
| Travellers | Bacterial infection (mostly acute); protozoal (amoebiasis, giardiasis); tropical sprue |
| Epidemics and outbreaks | Bacterial infection; epidemic idiopathic secretory diarrhoea (e.g. Brainerd diarrhoea); protozoal (cryptosporidiosis); viral (rotavirus, COVID-19) |
| Diabetes mellitus | Altered motility; associated coeliac disease, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, SIBO; drugs (especially acarbose, metformin) |
| AIDS | Drug side-effects; lymphoma; opportunistic infections (cryptosporidiosis, CMV, HSV, Mycobacterium avium complex) |
| Institutionalised / hospitalised | C. difficile colitis; drug side-effects; faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea; ischaemic colitis; tube feeding |

entries.title: Post-infectious IBS: treatable causes to look for
entries.body:
- Some cases are due to **bacterial overgrowth** and may respond to non-absorbable antibiotics; others are due to **acquired bile acid malabsorption**.
- **Coeliac disease** can first appear after an intestinal infection, so screen for it in this setting.

entries.title: Maldigestion versus malabsorption
entries.body:
- **Maldigestion** is defective intraluminal hydrolysis of nutrients; **malabsorption** is defective mucosal absorption. Their presentations and complications are similar.
- Many malabsorptive disorders, including coeliac disease, present **subtly** or mainly with **extra-intestinal** features rather than diarrhoea or steatorrhoea. Malabsorption may even be only a laboratory finding.

entries.title: Coeliac disease: why each extra-intestinal feature occurs
entries.body:
Table: Selected manifestations and probable causes (GIT Internal Med p. 66)
| Manifestation | Probable cause |
| Dermatitis herpetiformis | Epidermal (type 3) tTG autoimmunity |
| Ecchymoses, petechiae | Vitamin K deficiency; rarely thrombocytopenia |
| Oedema | Hypoproteinaemia |
| Thrombocytosis, Howell–Jolly bodies | Hyposplenism |
| Secondary hyperparathyroidism | Calcium and/or vitamin D malabsorption with hypocalcaemia |
| Osteopenia, osteomalacia, osteoporosis | Ca/vitamin D malabsorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism, chronic inflammation |
| Elevated liver tests | Lymphocytic hepatitis |
| Peripheral neuropathy | Vitamin B12 and thiamine deficiency; immune-based neurological dysfunction |
| Ataxia | Cerebellar and posterior column damage |
| Short stature, delayed puberty, amenorrhoea, infertility | Malnutrition; hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction |
| Weakness | Generalised muscle atrophy, hypokalaemia |

entries.title: Coeliac disease: wider associations and later risks
entries.body:
- **Further associated conditions** (besides type 1 diabetes and autoimmune liver and thyroid disease): Addison disease, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, **IgA deficiency**, **Down syndrome**, cystic fibrosis, Sjögren syndrome, **microscopic colitis**, epilepsy with cerebral calcification, sarcoidosis, recurrent pericarditis, iridocyclitis/choroiditis, some lung diseases (fibrosing alveolitis, idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis, bird-fancier's lung, cavitary lung disease) and macroamylasaemia.
- **Increased morbidity after diagnosis:** malignancy (non-Hodgkin lymphoma, **small-intestinal adenocarcinoma**); cardiovascular (ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, atrial fibrillation, dilated cardiomyopathy); respiratory (COPD, asthma, tuberculosis, influenza).

entries.title: Interpreting the general tests of absorption
entries.body:
- **Quantitative stool fat:** a borderline 8–14 g/24 h can occur in secretory or osmotic diarrhoea **not** caused by malabsorption. False negative if fat intake is inadequate; false positive with mineral-oil laxatives or rectal suppositories (e.g. cocoa butter).
- **Acid steatocrit:** a cheap, easy screening test for fat malabsorption; normal < 10%.
- **D-xylose test** (used in the book's algorithm, Fig 5.9): tests small-intestinal **mucosal** absorption, so it separates mucosal malabsorption from pancreatic insufficiency. Oral 25 g D-xylose; normal is > 4 g excreted in the urine over 5 h. False positives with renal failure, ascites or incomplete urine collection; it may also be abnormal in bacterial overgrowth and normal in mild or limited mucosal disease.
- **Lactose H₂ breath test:** a **late** peak (3–6 h) of > 20 ppm suggests lactose malabsorption.
- **Faecal elastase-1:** as sensitive as the secretin test for moderate-to-severe pancreatic insufficiency, but unreliable in mild insufficiency; false positives with high stool volume and mucosal disease. The **secretin test** is sensitive but labour-intensive and invasive.

entries.title: Diagnosing bacterial overgrowth
entries.body:
- **Gold standard:** quantitative culture of jejunal aspirate; > 10⁵ CFU/mL suggests overgrowth. False negatives occur with focal diverticula or overgrowth distal to the aspiration site.
- **Glucose H₂ breath test:** an **early** peak (within 2 h) of > 20 ppm suggests overgrowth. Contrast this with the **late** peak of lactose malabsorption. False negatives occur with non-hydrogen-producing organisms.
- **¹⁴C-D-xylose breath test:** sensitivity and specificity > 90%, and more specific than the H₂ breath test. A non-radioactive ¹³C version is suitable for children and pregnant women.

entries.title: Biopsy and ileal-function tests
entries.body:
- **Small-bowel biopsy:** distal duodenal specimens are usually adequate; take several (4–5). Biopsy is **diagnostic** in intestinal infection, Whipple disease, abetalipoproteinaemia, agammaglobulinaemia, lymphangiectasia, lymphoma and amyloidosis. In coeliac disease and tropical sprue the findings are characteristic, but the diagnosis rests on **improvement after treatment**.
- **Permeability studies** are gaining favour for screening for small-intestinal disease and monitoring the response to treatment.
- **SeHCAT:** 7-day retention **< 10%** is abnormal and indicates bile acid malabsorption; liver disease and bacterial overgrowth can give false results.
- The **Schilling test** is no longer used.

entries.title: History and examination clues
entries.body:
- In **acute-onset** constipation, always ask whether the patient can **pass gas**. Failure to pass gas can signal bowel obstruction.
- **Obstipation** is severe or complete constipation with practically no stool and **no flatus**. It may come with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, and points to obstruction.
- **DRE while bearing down:** pelvic floor dyssynergia is suggested when the anal sphincter **fails to relax** or the perineum **does not descend**.

entries.title: What anorectal testing measures
entries.body:
- **Anorectal manometry:** a pressure-sensitive catheter in the anorectum measures **resting and squeeze pressures** of the anal canal. It assesses the internal and external anal sphincters, **rectal sensation** and expulsion patterns.
- Defecography can also be performed with **MRI** (MRI defecography).

topics.title: Disorders of gut–brain interaction and IBS

entries.title: IBS: extra points
entries.body:
- **Functional chest pain of presumed oesophageal origin** is another oesophageal DGBI: chronic, recurrent pain or discomfort referred to the retrosternum.
- **Autonomic dysfunction** is also listed among the possible contributors to IBS.
- **History:** fibromyalgia is one of the associations found in IBS patients.
- **Limited laboratory tests:** besides faecal calprotectin and coeliac serology, GIT Internal Med lists **CBC** (anaemia or infection), **ESR and CRP** (inflammation) and **TSH** (thyroid dysfunction).

entries.title: Why probiotics are not used in IBS
entries.body: Probiotics are not prescribed in IBS because of a **lack of evidence supporting their efficacy**. This is the reason behind the book's "no routine recommendation".

entries.title: Salmonella culture and sugar fermentation
entries.body:
- A **facultative anaerobe** that grows well at **37 °C in 24 hours**. Colonies on MacConkey are **pale (yellow)** because it does not ferment lactose.
- Most species ferment sugars with **acid and gas**. **S. typhi makes acid only** (no gas).

entries.title: How the first-week blood culture is done
entries.body: Blood is cultured in **fluid (broth) media**, then **subcultured on solid media**, mainly MacConkey, at 37 °C.

entries.title: Control starts with food handlers
entries.body: **Food handlers are examined to detect carriers.** Carriers are treated or kept away from handling food. GIT Others lists this before immunisation.

entries.title: S. typhimurium food poisoning is self-limiting
entries.body: After lasting 2–5 days, **it usually resolves on its own (spontaneous cure)**.

entries.title: Campylobacter laboratory details
entries.body:
- A **rectal swab** is an acceptable specimen, collected with care to avoid oxygen exposure.
- Darting motility is seen in a wet mount under **dark-field illumination**.
- Isolated colonies are identified by **biotyping, serotyping and phage typing**.

entries.title: Brucella needs CO₂
entries.body: Brucella is aerobic, but culture needs **10% CO₂** as well as serum-enriched media.

entries.title: Extra radiological and endoscopic clues
entries.body:
- On radiology, **"collar-button" ulcers** are common in UC and only occasional in Crohn's disease.
- **Colonoscopy (the book's "Endoscopy" heading has no text):**
  - UC: friable mucosa, extensive ulceration and exudates.
  - Crohn's disease: a **single aphthous ulcer** is the earliest finding; multiple oedematous inflammatory polyps give the **cobblestone** appearance.

entries.title: More conditions that mimic IBD
entries.body:
- Other colitides: **radiation colitis**, **Behçet's colitis**, **schistosomiasis**, and sexually transmitted colitis (gonococcus, *Chlamydia*, herpes, trauma).
- Bacterial colitis also includes **Shigella** and **invasive E. coli**.
- Crohn's look-alikes: **lymphoma, Yersinia and tuberculosis**.

entries.title: The missing drug groups and a severity ladder
entries.body:
GIT Internal Med lists six drug groups for IBD. Two of them, **5-aminosalicylates (5-ASA/sulfasalazine)** and **probiotics/prebiotics**, do not appear in the book's IBD chapter. It also steps treatment up with severity:
Table: Stepwise IBD therapy (GIT Internal Med p. 81)
| Severity | Treatment |
| Mild | 5-aminosalicylates / sulfasalazine; local steroid enemas; local 5-ASA enemas and suppositories |
| Moderate | Prednisolone; budesonide; immunosuppressant |
| Severe | Biological therapy; surgery |

entries.title: 5-ASA and budesonide: the formulation decides where the drug acts
entries.body:
Choose the formulation by disease site. Most act in the colon; Pentasa is released from the duodenum onwards; enemas reach the rectum and sigmoid, and suppositories the rectum.

entries.title: Complications grouped by disease
entries.body:
- **UC:** toxic megacolon and malignancy.
- **Crohn's disease:** abscesses and fistulas, obstruction, and perianal disease.

entries.title: Polyp type in FAP
entries.body: In FAP, **most of the polyps are tubular adenomas**.

entries.title: Adenocarcinoma: 98% of large-bowel cancers
entries.body: The book says "more than 90%" of colorectal carcinomas are adenocarcinomas. GIT Others gives a precise figure: **98%** of all cancers of the large intestine are adenocarcinomas.

entries.title: Two kinds of mucoid (mucinous) carcinoma
entries.body:
- **Mucinous adenocarcinoma**: abundant *extracellular* mucin (the book: >50% mucinous material).
- **Signet ring cell carcinoma**: the mucin stays *inside* the malignant cell and pushes the nucleus to one side (eccentric nucleus).

entries.title: Add irradiation to the predisposing factors
entries.body: GIT Others lists **irradiation** as a predisposing factor for colorectal adenocarcinoma, along with adenoma, familial polyposis, IBD and gene mutations. It is not in the book's list.

entries.title: Principal liver functions
entries.body: Bile formation and secretion; metabolism of carbohydrates, amino acids, lipids and water- and fat-soluble vitamins; inactivation of ammonia (urea cycle), toxins, steroids and other hormones; synthesis of acute-phase proteins, albumin, clotting factors and steroid/hormone-binding proteins; immune function (Kupffer cells).

entries.title: Metabolic zonation of the lobule
entries.body: The **periportal** zone carries out gluconeogenesis and cholesterol and urea synthesis; the **pericentral** zone carries out glycolysis and glutamine and bile-acid synthesis.

topics.title: Symptoms and signs of chronic liver disease

entries.title: Palmar erythema and spider naevi: what they are
entries.body: Palmar erythema is persistent redness of the palms; spider naevi are small red skin marks caused by dilated capillaries near the skin surface.

entries.title: Hyperdynamic circulation and its vasodilators
entries.body:
- **Signs:** flushed extremities, bounding pulses and capillary pulsations, with increased portal blood flow, low blood pressure and reduced systemic vascular resistance; cardiac output rises.
- **The vasodilators are probably multiple:** formed by the sick hepatocyte, not inactivated by it, or bypassing it through intra- or extra-hepatic portosystemic shunts. They activate the sympathetic and renin–angiotensin systems, promoting sodium and water retention and ascites.
- **Nitric oxide** (endothelium-derived, potent vasodilator) is implicated in the hyperdynamic circulation and is important in ascites, hepatorenal syndrome and portal hypertension. Prostanoids released into the portal vein and endocannabinoids are also shown as splanchnic vasodilators.

entries.title: Hepatocellular failure: when it occurs
entries.body: Hepatocellular failure complicates almost all liver diseases but **not portal venous occlusion alone**; it may be the terminal event in chronic cholestasis such as primary biliary cirrhosis. Its picture and treatment are similar whatever the cause.

entries.title: What the liver makes, and what albumin and PT tell you
entries.body:
- The liver synthesises albumin, **all clotting factors except factor VIII**, carrier proteins (ceruloplasmin, transferrin), cholesterol, bile salts and urea.
- The source links the bleeding tendency of chronic liver disease to failed synthesis of fibrinogen and factors II, V, VII, IX, XI, XII and XIII.
- A falling serum albumin is an excellent indicator of severity and prognosis in chronic liver disease. PT depends on factors I, II, V, VII and X; because these have a shorter half-life than albumin, PT is an **earlier** indicator of severe liver injury.

entries.title: Liver tests grouped by what they reflect
entries.body:
- **Excretory / detoxification:** serum and urine bilirubin, serum ammonia.
- **Liver-cell injury:** AST, ALT.
- **Cholestasis:** ALP, GGT, 5′-nucleotidase. 5′-nucleotidase is more specific for cholestasis than ALP but is not widely used.
- **Synthetic function:** albumin, coagulation factors.

entries.title: ALP and GGT with space-occupying or infiltrative lesions
entries.body:
- ALP and GGT are markedly raised (>3-fold) not only in cholestasis but also with **space-occupying lesions and hepatic infiltration** (tumours such as cancer, cysts, lymph nodes). Non-hepatic ALP rises occur in bone disease (rickets, osteomalacia).
- In infiltration, bilirubin may be **normal**: partial obstruction lets bilirubin pass yet stimulates ALP/GGT synthesis. AST/ALT are normal or slightly raised (AST > ALT). AFP rises in HCC, and CEA with secondaries from GIT cancer.

entries.title: Causes of an isolated ALP rise
entries.body: Primary or metastatic hepatic tumours, granulomatous liver disease, primary biliary cirrhosis, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, hyperthyroidism, bone disease with rapid turnover, sclerosing cholangitis.

entries.title: Where bilirubin comes from
entries.body: About 250–300 mg of bilirubin is produced daily; 70–80% comes from haemoglobin of senescent red cells, the rest from prematurely destroyed erythroid cells in the marrow and turnover of haemoproteins such as myoglobin. It is formed in reticuloendothelial cells, mainly in the spleen and liver.

entries.title: Hepatocyte handling in four steps
entries.body: Uptake, cytosolic binding, conjugation, secretion: albumin-bound bilirubin is taken up (albumin is not), binds **ligandin (Z protein)**, is conjugated to glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyl transferase in the endoplasmic reticulum, and mono- and diglucuronides are actively transported into bile.

entries.title: In the gut
entries.body:
- Conjugated bilirubin is not absorbed by the intestinal mucosa; only in the distal ileum and colon is it hydrolysed (bacterial β-glucuronidases) to unconjugated bilirubin, then reduced to colourless urobilinogens.
- The primary bile acids, cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid, are made from cholesterol, secreted in bile, and mostly reabsorbed in the ileum for re-secretion (enterohepatic circulation).

entries.title: Haemolytic, obstructive and hepatic jaundice: details the book's comparison lacks
entries.body:
- Urine **bile salts** (with bilirubin) are absent in haemolytic jaundice and present in obstructive and hepatic jaundice. In hepatic jaundice the stool is **clay-coloured**, as in obstruction.
- In haemolytic jaundice, evidence of haemolysis includes raised reticulocytes **and raised LDH** (the LDH–haptoglobin–reticulocyte algorithm is in Chapter 29). Obstructive jaundice raises serum cholesterol and **β-lipoproteins**.

entries.title: Crigler–Najjar II, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor
entries.body:
- Crigler–Najjar **type II** = partial UGT deficiency, bilirubin <20 mg/dL (type I: complete absence, >20 mg/dL).
- Dubin–Johnson (defect of bilirubin secretion) has a **darkly pigmented** liver; Rotor syndrome is usually asymptomatic with a non-pigmented liver.

entries.title: Reading HBV serology
entries.body:
Table: HBV serology panels
| HBsAg | Anti-HBc | IgM anti-HBc | Anti-HBs | Interpretation |
| − | − | | − | Susceptible |
| + | + | + | − | Acutely infected |
| + | + | − | − | Chronically infected |
| − | + | | + | Immune: natural infection |
| − | − | | + | Immune: vaccination |
- **Acute vs chronic vs past HBV:** HBeAg and HBV DNA are + early then − in acute infection, ± in chronic, − in past; anti-HBe is − early then + (acute), ± (chronic), + (past); ALT is markedly raised (acute), mildly–moderately raised (chronic), normal (past).
- An **isolated anti-HBc** in the window period usually means a resolving acute infection that is **not yet completely resolved**, because anti-HBs has not yet appeared.

entries.title: Normal ALT/AST does not prove recovery
entries.body: In hepatitis B and C, normal ALT/AST does not prove recovery: replication may persist, so clearance must be shown serologically.

entries.title: HAV RNA in faeces
entries.body: HAV can be detected by **PCR on faeces**, earlier than serology, but this is very rarely performed.

entries.title: Anti-HCV pitfalls
entries.body: A positive anti-HCV may be false (cross-reactivity with another infection) and must be confirmed by PCR; a negative result does not exclude HCV (immunodeficiency; very early infection before seroconversion: do PCR). **Anti-HCV IgM is not a marker of acute infection.**

entries.title: Hepatitis G
entries.body: Hepatitis G is spread by contaminated blood or blood products; prevalence in blood donors is about 1%.

entries.title: Chronic hepatitis at a glance
entries.body:
| | Autoimmune | HBV | HCV |
| Sex | Female | Male | Equal |
| Age | 15–25 y | Older | All ages |
| Associated autoimmune disease | Frequent | Rare | Occasional |
| Autoantibodies | High titre (ANA, ASMA, LKM) | Low / absent | Low / absent |
| Cancer risk | Low | High | High |

entries.title: How long acute viral hepatitis lasts
entries.body: Acute viral hepatitis usually resolves 4–8 weeks after symptom onset.

entries.title: PT, not ALT, judges severity
entries.body: Severity is judged by impaired synthetic function rather than ALT/AST levels: **PT** is the key prognostic indicator, and a PT more than 3 seconds above normal carries a poor prognosis.

entries.title: HBV is in every body fluid except stool
entries.body: HBV is present in all body fluids **except stool**, so spread is by blood or body-fluid contact.

entries.title: HCV and transfusion
entries.body: HCV (enveloped ssRNA flavivirus) is the most common cause of transfusion-associated hepatitis; sexual transmission is low.

entries.title: Why HDV needs HBV
entries.body: HDV causes infection only when it is **encapsulated with HBsAg**, which is the basis of its dependence on HBV.

entries.title: HEV genotypes and chronic HEV
entries.body: Genotypes 1 and 2 cause waterborne outbreaks; genotypes 3 and 4 cause sporadic cases, including via undercooked meat such as pork. HEV affects mainly adults and is rare in children. Chronic (genotype 3) hepatitis E occurs only in the immunocompromised: organ-transplant recipients, cancer chemotherapy, HIV.

entries.title: Rosettes in severe chronic hepatitis
entries.body: In severe chronic hepatitis, fibrous septa extend into the lobule, producing **rosette formation** as well as bridging fibrosis.

entries.title: Who becomes a carrier, and what follows
entries.body: Chronic HBV is more common in males. About 50% of HBsAg carriers have evidence of replication (HBeAg / HBV DNA positive), and about 20% of carriers develop cirrhosis within 5 years of disease onset.

entries.title: Loss of immune tolerance
entries.body: Immune-tolerant patients (mostly infected perinatally) often lose tolerance in the 3rd–5th decade, when acute hepatitis develops and chronic hepatitis may follow.

entries.title: Inactive carriers and reactivation
entries.body: Inactive carriers are usually discovered on screening before blood donation. Reactivation can occur with cancer chemotherapy or bone-marrow transplantation, so **antiviral prophylaxis is indicated** in these settings.

entries.title: HBeAg loss
entries.body: When HBeAg disappears, remission is usually sustained for many years.

entries.title: Pegylated interferon: who responds
entries.body: Pegylated interferon α-2a for 48 weeks gives response rates of about 25–45%; response is best in younger patients with ALT about 3× the upper limit of normal.

entries.title: Entecavir, tenofovir and lamivudine
entries.body:
- **Entecavir:** HBV DNA becomes negative by 48 weeks in 67% (HBeAg-positive) and 90% (HBeAg-negative).
- **Tenofovir** can be used for lamivudine mutations but not alone for adefovir mutations.
- **Lamivudine** (100 mg/day) is well tolerated but limited by resistance from the **YMDD mutant**.

entries.title: How DAAs work
entries.body: DAAs target specific HCV **non-structural (NS) proteins** vital for viral replication, disrupting replication and infection.

entries.title: Sofosbuvir and ribavirin: dose and adverse effects
entries.body:
- **Sofosbuvir:** 400 mg once daily with or without food; adverse effects (~10%) fatigue, headache, anorexia, insomnia.
- **Ribavirin** (adjuvant): 600–1200 mg/day by weight; adverse effects haemolytic anaemia, teratogenicity, sperm abnormalities.

entries.title: Why Egypt's HCV burden is so high
entries.body: Egypt's HCV burden also reflects nosocomial spread through inadequately disinfected equipment (e.g. circumcision, dental practice), besides the antischistosomal injection campaigns.

entries.title: Type 1 vs type 2 AIH
entries.body:
| | Type 1 | Type 2 |
| Autoantibodies | ANA alone 10% · ASMA alone 35% · both 50% · neither 5% | LKM-1, LC-1 |
| Serum IgG | +++ | + |
| Usual age | 10 years to elderly | 2–18 years |
| Progression to cirrhosis | ≈45% | ≈80% |
How common each type is has been left out: the source and the book give different figures (review point R25).

entries.title: Weight loss should be gradual
entries.body: Weight loss should be gradual, **not more than 1.6 kg per week**, because rapid weight loss increases fibrosis.

entries.title: Cryptogenic cirrhosis
entries.body: Some cirrhosis is **cryptogenic** (no identifiable cause).

entries.title: Two routes by which cirrhosis causes disease
entries.body:
- **Altered hepatic blood flow:** portal hypertension → variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy; ascites → SBP, HRS.
- **Reduced functional cell mass:** less detoxification of bilirubin, ammonia and drugs; less albumin and clotting-protein synthesis.

entries.title: Associations, fever and feminisation
entries.body: Recurrent pancreatitis (especially in alcoholics) is among the associated conditions. Fever may be due to portal bacteraemia or liver-cell necrosis, not only infection. Feminisation in males is seen in long-standing cases and usually indicates **decompensation**.

entries.title: Urine urobilinogen
entries.body: Urine urobilinogen is increased in cirrhosis.

entries.title: Elastography cut-offs
entries.body:
- Liver stiffness **≤20 kPa with platelets >150 × 10⁹/L**: screening endoscopy not needed (large varices <5%).
- Liver stiffness **>25 kPa** is sufficient to diagnose clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), with no endoscopy needed; treat with carvedilol to reduce the risk of decompensation.

entries.title: PBC: supplements and biopsy
entries.body: Supplement fat-soluble vitamins and calcium. Biopsy shows loss of small bile ducts with **ductular proliferation**.

entries.title: Haemochromatosis: skin, cancer risk and MRI
entries.body:
- Bronze skin is due to **melanin** deposition; about 30% may develop HCC as a complication of cirrhosis.
- MRI showing iron in the **pancreas** distinguishes hereditary haemochromatosis from secondary iron overload (haemosiderosis), where only the liver is affected.

entries.title: Wilson disease: copper handling and features
entries.body:
- Ceruloplasmin is an α2-globulin carrying six copper atoms (loaded by ATP7B); 50–75% of intestinal copper is absorbed; normal serum ceruloplasmin is 20–35 mg/dL.
- Haemolysis is due to the toxic effect of copper on red cells; psychiatric disease can extend to psychosis (schizophrenia-like or manic-depressive).
- Kayser–Fleischer rings are gold or greenish-gold rings at the corneoscleral junction; in a few people they are the **first sign** of Wilson disease.

entries.title: Causes by site that the book does not list
entries.body:
| Site | Additional causes in the source |
| Increased flow | Idiopathic tropical splenomegaly; arteriovenous fistula |
| Prehepatic | Splenic-vein thrombosis; invasion or compression of portal/splenic vein by tumour |
| Presinusoidal | Early PBC; chronic active hepatitis; vinyl chloride, copper; idiopathic portal hypertension |
| Sinusoidal (non-cirrhotic) | Cytotoxic drugs; vitamin A intoxication |
| Post-sinusoidal | Alcoholic central hyaline sclerosis |
| Posthepatic | IVC webs, tumour invasion or thrombosis |

entries.title: Why the spleen enlarges
entries.body: Splenomegaly results from congestion **and** reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia.

entries.title: Variceal haemorrhage as a cause of death
entries.body: Variceal haemorrhage accounts for about **one-third** of deaths in cirrhosis with portal hypertension.

entries.title: How non-selective β-blockers work
entries.body: Non-selective β-blockers reduce portal inflow by lowering cardiac output (β1) and blocking β2 vasodilator receptors on splanchnic arteries; they are **as effective as banding**. Propranolol alternative: 80–160 mg/day, titrated to cut resting pulse by 25%, for life.

entries.title: Blood-pressure target and terlipressin regimen
entries.body:
- Resuscitate to a systolic BP of about 100 mmHg.
- Terlipressin: 2 mg IV every 6 h, then 1 mg every 4 h, for 2–5 days. The book gives the duration (2–5 days) but no dose; this dose is from the Hepatology source only. (That source's next sentence on ischaemic heart disease is garbled; see note N4.)

entries.title: Histoacryl and balloon tamponade
entries.body: Histoacryl (tissue adhesive) is used for gastric varices **and big oesophageal varices**. Balloon tamponade is rarely used now because of its complications, but it can be used when endoscopic or vasoconstrictor therapy has failed or is unavailable.

entries.title: TIPS timing and surgical shunts
entries.body:
- The source gives both steps together: a rebleed within 10 days is treated by repeating endoscopic therapy (as in the book, p. 316), and **TIPS** is used when bleeding cannot be stopped or early rebleeding occurs **within 5 days** of endoscopic therapy.
- Surgical shunts are usually end-to-side portocaval or Warren (splenorenal).

entries.title: Commonest causes after cirrhosis
entries.body: After cirrhosis, malignancy is the next commonest cause; cardiac failure and tuberculous peritonitis are less frequent.

entries.title: Causes grouped by portal hypertension
entries.body:
| | Causes |
| With PHT: intrahepatic | Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, active chronic hepatitis, liver failure, veno-occlusive disease, liver tumour, schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis, Budd–Chiari, focal nodular hyperplasia |
| With PHT: extrahepatic | Heart failure, pericarditis, portal-vein thrombosis |
| No PHT: peritoneal | Carcinomatosis, mesothelioma, pseudomyxoma, infection |
| No PHT: hypoalbuminaemia | Nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, bowel disease |
| No PHT: mixed | Myxoedema, pancreatic/biliary ascites, amyloidosis, familial Mediterranean fever, granulomatous disease |

entries.title: RAAS: one activation, two consequences
entries.body: Renin (juxtaglomerular cells) converts liver-made angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE (mainly pulmonary endothelium) forms angiotensin II, a pressor that also releases aldosterone. Release is driven by renal perfusion (JG cells), distal Na/Cl load (macula densa) and sympathetic β-receptors. The same RAAS activation causes **renal sodium avidity (ascites)** and **renal vasoconstriction (HRS)**.

entries.title: Detecting and tapping ascites
entries.body:
- Ultrasound detects as little as 30 mL (right lateral decubitus).
- Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated for new-onset ascites or a suspected complication (sterile, 20–23-gauge angiocatheter).
- Extra fluid tests: Gram stain, triglycerides (chylous), bilirubin (bowel perforation), glucose, amylase, LDH, cytology. Pair ascitic with same-day serum albumin for SAAG.

entries.title: SAAG: accuracy and extra causes
entries.body:
SAAG correlates directly with portal pressure; ≥1.1 g/dL (11 g/L) vs <1.1 separates portal-hypertensive ascites with >97% accuracy.
- **Extra high-gradient causes:** fatty liver of pregnancy, massive metastases, mixed ascites, myxoedema, portal-vein thrombosis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.
- **Extra low-gradient causes:** bowel obstruction/infarction, postoperative lymphatic leak, serositis in connective-tissue disease.

entries.title: Diuretics: sodium intake, timing and when to stop
entries.body: The book already gives bed rest, daily weight and spironolactone 100–200 mg. The source adds a **70–90 mmol sodium diet**; **after 4 days** consider adding furosemide 40 mg daily; and **stop diuretics** if pre-coma (flap), hypokalaemia, azotaemia or alkalosis.

entries.title: Refractory ascites: two kinds, and what drives it
entries.body: Refractory ascites (10–20% of patients) is diuretic-**resistant** (no response to maximal doses) or diuretic-**intractable** (complications prevent an effective dose). Look for contributors: worsening liver disease, portal/hepatic-vein thrombosis, GI bleeding, infection/SBP, malnutrition, HCC, cardiac or renal disease, hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic substances.

entries.title: Large-volume paracentesis, TIPS and shunting
entries.body: Large-volume paracentesis: 4–6 L daily until the abdomen is emptied, repeated every 2–4 weeks; continue diuretics and sodium restriction afterwards. (Albumin replacement, 8 g per litre removed, is on book p. 342 and in the source.) TIPS lowers diuretic needs, renin and aldosterone but may precipitate encephalopathy or liver failure. Peritoneovenous shunting is another option.

entries.title: Who gets SBP, and which organisms
entries.body: Infection of ascitic fluid may be spontaneous or follow a previous paracentesis. The **spontaneous** type develops in about **8% of cirrhotics with ascites** (the book's 10% is for all cirrhotic patients, a figure the source also gives), especially when the cirrhosis is severely decompensated. 90% are monomicrobial. More than one organism suggests paracentesis-related infection; anaerobes are rare. Variceal bleeding and previous SBP carry particular risk.

entries.title: From translocation to SBP
entries.body: Gut bacteria translocate (overgrowth, dysmotility) to mesenteric nodes or bypass liver RES via portosystemic shunts → bacteraemia → **bacterascites**, which resolves if ascitic opsonic activity is good and becomes SBP if it is poor.

entries.title: SBP can be silent
entries.body: Classic features (fever, pain, leucocytosis) **may be absent**; the book (p. 343) already says to suspect SBP in any cirrhotic with ascites who deteriorates.

entries.title: Treatment length and prophylaxis after bleeding
entries.body: Treat for ≥5 days; amoxicillin–clavulanate is as effective as third-generation cephalosporins. After upper GI haemorrhage (or sclerotherapy) give norfloxacin 400 mg 12-hourly for **at least 7 days**.

entries.title: The kidneys are normal: the defect is blood flow
entries.body: The book (p. 346) gives the normal renal histology, renal vasoconstriction and splanchnic vasodilatation. The source adds that the kidneys are **capable of normal function** (HRS is progressive, and the defect is renal blood flow), that **cardiac dysfunction** is a third component, and that most patients have tense ascites.

entries.title: Classic criteria and what to exclude
entries.body: Classic criteria used serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL (133 µmol/L) persisting 48 h after diuretic withdrawal and albumin expansion. Exclude toxins (paracetamol, NSAIDs, carbon tetrachloride), infection, ATN (hypotension, aminoglycosides, contrast) and obstructive uropathy.

entries.title: Preventing HRS
entries.body: Avoid volume depletion (diuretics, lactulose, GI bleeding, LVP without albumin); use ACEI/ARB/NSAIDs/antibiotics judiciously; treat infection early and give SBP prophylaxis; pentoxifylline in severe alcoholic hepatitis; prevent variceal bleeding.

entries.title: Albumin loading and alternatives to terlipressin
entries.body:
- Albumin loading 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g) to a CVP of 10–15 cmH₂O.
- Alternatives to terlipressin: midodrine 2.5–5 mg tds (to 15 mg tds) + octreotide 100 µg SC tds (to 200 µg), or noradrenaline 0.1–0.7 µg/kg/min, titrated to MAP.
- Vasopressors generally for up to 2 weeks; evaluate for transplantation.
The terlipressin escalation schedule and maintenance albumin dose from the same table differ from the book and are kept for review (R36).

entries.title: Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinaemia: the algorithm
entries.body: First exclude recent trauma, haematoma or transfusion; then LDH, haptoglobin and reticulocyte count: abnormal → haemolysis/dyserythropoiesis; normal → Gilbert or Crigler–Najjar I/II.

entries.title: Halothane
entries.body: Halothane (like paracetamol) causes toxic hepatitis with mixed (hepatic) hyperbilirubinaemia.

entries.title: Biliary obstruction vs liver disease
entries.body:
| | Favours biliary obstruction | Favours liver disease |
| History | Abdominal pain, fever/rigors, prior biliary surgery, older age | Viral prodrome, known viral exposure, blood products or IV drug use, hepatotoxin, family history |
| Examination | Fever, tenderness, palpable mass, surgical scar | Spider telangiectasias, stigmata of portal hypertension, asterixis |
| Laboratory | ALP ↑ out of proportion; PT normal or corrects with vitamin K; leucocytosis; amylase/lipase ↑ | Aminotransferases ↑ out of proportion; PT does not correct with vitamin K; thrombocytopenia; positive serology |

entries.title: Intrahepatic cholestasis by level
entries.body:
- **Hepatocyte:** viral, drug and alcoholic hepatitis; post-necrotic cirrhosis; endotoxin.
- **Canaliculus:** benign recurrent cholestasis; hormones, pregnancy, drugs.
- **Ductules:** PBC, allograft rejection, **graft-versus-host**, biliary atresia, idiopathic adult ductopenia.
- **Larger ducts:** primary/secondary sclerosing cholangitis.

entries.title: Ammonia
entries.body: About half of gut ammonia is made by bacteria, the rest from dietary protein and glutamine; it is cleared as urea and glutamine. Blood ammonia is raised in **90%** of HE; ammonia damages the blood–brain barrier and astrocytes and shifts neural activity toward inhibition. Reduced muscle metabolism also raises it.

entries.title: Amino-acid imbalance and false neurotransmitters
entries.body: Aromatic amino acids rise (failed hepatic deamination) while branched-chain amino acids fall (muscle/renal uptake driven by **hyperinsulinaemia**); more aromatic amino acids enter the brain, and phenylalanine inhibits dopa synthesis → false neurotransmitters.

entries.title: GABA
entries.body: GABA is made by gut bacteria and normally cleared by the liver; in liver failure or shunting it reaches the systemic circulation.

entries.title: Three strategies
entries.body: Treat the **precipitating cause**; reduce production and absorption of gut-derived ammonia and toxins; modify neurotransmitter balance.

entries.title: Cerebral blood flow in acute liver failure
entries.body: Cerebral blood flow is generally increased: persistent vasodilatation and loss of autoregulation cause hyperaemia, and the rise in cerebral blood volume can worsen brain oedema.

reviews.title: Misoprostol: a PGE₁ or a PGE₂ analogue?

reviews.title: H. pylori triple therapy: duration and first-line status

positions.label: Book p. 41
positions.text: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for **14 days**, but **no longer recommended as empirical first-line** unless local clarithromycin resistance is known to be low.

positions.label: Book p. 48

positions.label: GIT Internal Med p. 31

reviews.title: Levofloxacin dose in the rescue regimen

positions.label: Book p. 41

positions.label: Book p. 48 · GIT Others p. 5

reviews.note: The book's two pages disagree with each other; GIT Others agrees with p. 48.

reviews.title: Transfusion threshold in acute upper GI bleeding
reviews.from: Integration review of GIT Internal Med companion ledger row GB-08

positions.label: GIT Internal Med p. 39
positions.text: Transfuse for shock **or Hb < 10** with recent or active bleeding. The source prints the unit as "mg/dl".

positions.label: Book pp. 50–51
positions.text: "IV fluids and blood transfusion **when indicated**"; "Hemoglobin levels are generally a **poor indicator** of the need to transfuse". No numeric threshold is given.

reviews.note: For variceal bleeding the book (Ch 23, p. 315) uses a restrictive target of Hb 7–8 g/dL (see R32). The shock criteria from the same source page are taught in Chapter 3; the Hb threshold is not.

reviews.title: Commonest site of gastric cancer: how common?

positions.label: Book p. 62
positions.text: Antrum/pyloric area **60%**, body 15%, fundus 25%.

positions.label: GIT Others p. 15
positions.text: Pyloric region **50%**, then **lesser curvature 25%**; it can occur anywhere in the stomach.

reviews.note: Both agree that the pyloric (antral) region is the commonest site; the percentages and the second site differ.

reviews.title: How long is "acute" diarrhoea?

positions.label: Book p. 77
positions.text: Acute diarrhoea lasts **less than 2 to 3 weeks or, rarely, 6 to 8 weeks**.

positions.label: GIT Internal Med p. 51
positions.text: Acute diarrhoea lasts **less than 4 weeks**.

reviews.note: Both agree that diarrhoea lasting more than 4 weeks is evaluated as chronic.

reviews.title: Stool fat and lactose breath test protocols

positions.label: GIT Internal Med pp. 69–70 (tables)
positions.text: **100 g** fat diet with stool collected over **3 days**; lactose dose **1 g/kg** body weight.

reviews.note: The source's text and tables disagree with each other; the book follows the text.

reviews.title: IBS diagnostic criteria: which Rome edition?

positions.label: Book p. 102 (Rome V)
positions.text: Pain on average **at least 3 days per month** over the last 3 months.

positions.label: GIT Internal Med p. 75 (Rome IV)
positions.text: Recurrent abdominal pain **at least 1 day per week** in the last 3 months.

reviews.note: The 2-of-3 associated features (related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form) are the same in both.

reviews.title: Low-FODMAP diet: which foods to limit?

positions.label: Book p. 105

positions.label: GIT Internal Med p. 75

reviews.note: Both give lubiprostone (chloride channel activator) as the first option.

reviews.title: Widal test: what a high H titre means

positions.label: GIT Others p. 24
positions.text: "**More than one** H antigen (≥1:160) suggest recent infection with this type of Salmonella **and** recent immunization."

reviews.note: The GIT Others list here is garbled (its items 1–2 are cut off), so it is not a reliable correction.

reviews.title: PBC in the immunoglobulin list: raised AMA or raised IgM?

positions.label: Hepatology p. 11

reviews.title: What happens to the reabsorbed 10–20% of urobilinogen?

positions.label: Book p. 245
positions.text: The reabsorbed 10–20% **escape the enterohepatic circulation** and pass to the kidney to be excreted in urine.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 82
positions.text: The reabsorbed 10–20% enter the portal blood and are **re-excreted by the liver**; only a small fraction escapes hepatic uptake into urine (figure: ~80% faeces, ~18% enterohepatic, ~2% urine).

reviews.title: Gilbert's syndrome: decreased uptake or decreased conjugation?

positions.label: Book p. 245 (Ch 18)
positions.text: Gilbert's is listed under "II – Decrease uptake" ("defect of hepatic uptake and/or decrease of conjugation").

positions.label: Book pp. 350–351 (Ch 29) · Hepatology pp. 83–84
positions.text: Gilbert's is a **decreased conjugation** disorder (deficient hepatic bilirubin glucuronidation); drugs such as rifampin are the example of decreased uptake.

reviews.note: The book's two chapters classify it differently.

reviews.note: The Hepatology source itself also says rest is unhelpful for HAV (p. 24).

positions.text: **Two of three**: cholestatic ALP, AMA, compatible biopsy.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 51

reviews.title: UDCA in PBC: does it change the disease?

positions.label: Book p. 288
positions.text: UDCA is first-line; it improves biochemistry, **slows fibrosis progression and improves survival**.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 51

reviews.title: Alcohol threshold for alcoholic cirrhosis: grams or millilitres?

positions.label: Book p. 281 (also p. 298: >10 years, no amount) · Hepatology p. 44
positions.text: Regular intake **>30 ml/day** for more than 10 years.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 55
positions.text: At least **30 g** of alcohol daily for more than 10 years.

reviews.title: Transfusion target in acute variceal bleeding
reviews.from: Hepatology extras ledger D-24; the same text is in GIT Internal Med p. 43 (companion row GB-18, out of its scope)

positions.label: Book p. 315
positions.text: Transfusion should be **restrictive**, with a target haemoglobin generally around **7–8 g/dL**.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 61 · GIT Internal Med p. 43
positions.text: Over-transfusion may cause rebleeding; keep the **haematocrit around 30**.

reviews.note: Both warn against over-transfusion; the numeric targets differ.

reviews.title: Nasogastric (Ryle's) tube in GI bleeding: routine or selective?
reviews.from: Hepatology extras ledger D-25; GIT Internal Med companion GB-09 and GB-25 (context)

positions.label: Book p. 315 (variceal bleeding)
positions.text: A nasogastric tube may be considered **selectively** but is **not routinely required** in every patient.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 61 (variceal bleeding)
positions.text: Ryle's tube insertion for aspiration and lavage, listed as part of **routine** resuscitation.

positions.label: GIT Internal Med pp. 40, 46 (non-variceal and lower GI bleeding)
positions.text: A nasogastric tube for gastric wash and monitoring of ongoing bleeding; nasogastric lavage in the unstable patient with lower GI bleeding.

reviews.note: The book's Chapter 3 bleeding pages (pp. 50–53) do not mention a nasogastric tube. The GIT Internal Med uses are kept in Chapter 3 with this cross-reference.

reviews.title: Screening endoscopy for every cirrhotic?
reviews.from: Hepatology extras ledger D-26; the same sentence is in GIT Internal Med p. 43

positions.label: Book pp. 285, 313
positions.text: Assessment by non-invasive criteria and/or upper GI endoscopy; guided by **Baveno VII**, some patients can **safely avoid endoscopy**.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 60 · GIT Internal Med p. 43
positions.text: "**Every patient** diagnosed with cirrhosis should have an upper GI endoscopy".

reviews.note: The Hepatology source itself (p. 60) also gives the elastography criteria that spare endoscopy (taught in Chapter 22).

reviews.title: Blood count in amoebic liver abscess

positions.label: Book p. 331 (Ch 25)
positions.text: "CBC: Leukocytosis and **eosinophilia**".

positions.label: Book p. 138 (Ch 9) · GIT Others p. 47

reviews.title: Terlipressin escalation and albumin dose in HRS

positions.label: Book p. 347 · Hepatology text
positions.text: Terlipressin 1 mg q4–6h or 2 mg/day infusion; escalate if creatinine falls <25% **after 2 days**, to a maximum of 12 mg/day; albumin 20% at **20–40 g/day**.

positions.label: Hepatology p. 80 (image table)
positions.text: Start 1 mg IV every 4 h; increase up to 2 mg IV every 4 h if creatinine has not improved by 25% **at day 3**; maintenance albumin **20–60 g/day**.
